target_customer: Parents buying a $299 interactive robot toy for young children
problem: Young children lacked an expressive, playful robot companion that could see, hear, speak and move and that could be extended with apps and character skins.
business_model: Consumer hardware sold at about $299 with a planned app store, accessories and licensable character skins

founders.name: Bart Dirkx
founders.background_notes: Named as founder on the YC page. No background found in sources opened.

founders.name: Ruud van der Aalst
founders.background_notes: Named as founder on the YC page. No background found in sources opened.

exit.reason: Not stated by the company. A third party profile attributes it to high hardware costs and a long sales cycle.

competitors.name: Keepon
competitors.what: Soft, squishy dancing robot used as a comparison for the IXI-Play owl body

competitors.name: Furby
competitors.what: Interactive electronic toy creature that the article uses as a comparison

competitors.name: Tickle Me Elmo
competitors.what: Mass market interactive plush toy used as a comparison

technical_complexity.rationale: A two person team had to build a mechanical body with flexing motion, LCD eyes, Android software, camera vision for faces, cards and objects, speech recognition and touch sensing, plus a manufacturing run, all at a $299 target price.

defensibility.rationale: The Android based hardware used off the shelf components and the idea of character skins and an app store depended on content and distribution that did not yet exist. Larger toy makers could copy the format.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows an incumbent copying or buying it. The company appears to have gone inactive without an acquirer.

market_need_then: In 2013 smartphone based and social robots for children were drawing press and crowdfunding attention, and the company planned a crowdfunding campaign in summer 2013 to finance a first production run. Direct evidence of parent demand was not found.

identity.mascot_or_character: The robot is shaped like an owl with a soft flexing body and LCD eyes that show emotions (IEEE Spectrum, April 2013). A green robot owl is also shown in 2013 coverage of the Dutch company WittyWorX.
identity.visual_style: Toy like owl with customizable skins for different characters

branding.brand_signature: The expressive owl robot with changeable character skins

brand_strength.rationale: Only a handful of 2013 articles mention the product. No community, merch or brand coverage was found, and the name shares letters with unrelated IXI marks.

outcome_analysis: Ixiplay was a two person hardware team building a $299 Android owl robot for children, with a crowdfunding plan for the first production run. The company went inactive; the only cause found is a third party profile citing high hardware costs and a long sales cycle, so the failure factors are tentative and the cause is not public from primary sources.
notes: YC lists the website as empty, so there was no company site to fetch. Crunchbase snippet shows a seed stage entry with no readable amount, date or investors, so the round rests on one database with null fields. Loot Drop gives 2016 as end year and about 5.0M dollars burned; this rests on one aggregator and is unverified, so no amount is recorded. IEEE Spectrum names the company as the Dutch WittyWorX and states a crowdfunding plan; no source confirms the campaign happened. Unrelated IXI trademarks and IXI funding rounds in search results were excluded.
